concept.name: Short and distort
concept.definition: An illegal manipulation scheme that is the bearish mirror image of a pump and dump: the perpetrator establishes a short position in a stock, then spreads false or unsubstantiated negative rumors to drive the price down, and covers the short at the lower price for a profit. Spreading false information to move a price and manipulative short selling violate the antifraud provisions of the securities laws.
concept.intuition: Bet that a stock will fall, then poison the well with scary lies so it actually falls, and buy back cheap while everyone else panics.
concept.mechanics: The manipulator shorts the stock (sometimes using naked short sales), then disseminates fabricated negative claims — fake lawsuits, earnings warnings, regulatory actions — through social media, message boards, spam, or instant messages to traders. As the price falls on the false news, the short is covered profitably before the story is debunked.
concept.failure_modes: Legitimate short-seller research (e.g., critical reports by activist funds) sits close to the line: negative claims that turn out wrong but were made in good faith are not fraud, so cases hinge on proving falsity and intent; anonymity of online posts makes attribution difficult.
concept.misconceptions: Short selling combined with publishing negative opinions is not automatically short and distort — the scheme requires false or misleading statements; truthful bearish analysis, even aggressive, is lawful speech and often valuable price discovery.
concept.example: In 2008 the SEC charged trader Paul Berliner with securities fraud for spreading a false rumor via instant messages that the Blackstone-Alliance Data Systems deal was being renegotiated lower, while he held a short position in ADS; he settled with a $130,000 penalty and an industry bar.

citations.source: SEC Office of Investor Education and Assistance, Key Points About Regulation SHO
